idiom_name: class Mediator with dict[str, list[Callable]] and weak references for listeners
implementation_notes: Python makes the classic structure optional: a mediator is any object holding a dictionary of event name to callables, colleagues register bound methods or lambdas and call hub.notify(...) instead of each other. Duck typing replaces the Colleague base class, so the Colleague/ConcreteColleague distinction disappears and only the protocol remains - a docstring or a typing.Protocol is the contract. Because the hub holds listeners strongly, store weak references (weakref.WeakMethod, WeakSet, WeakValueDictionary) or unregister explicitly when the hub outlives the colleagues; the weakref documentation covers both the mechanism and its limits.
pitfalls: The hub holds listeners strongly by default, so a bound method registered on a long-lived mediator keeps the colleague alive; use weakref.WeakMethod/WeakSet or unsubscribe on teardown.
Dispatch is synchronous and exceptions propagate out of notify, so one failing listener prevents the rest from running; collect or log errors per listener.
Mutating the handler list during dispatch (a listener that unsubscribes) changes iteration; dispatch over a copy.
The GIL serialises synchronous handlers and notify is still a dict lookup plus a loop, so keep payloads small and keep the hub off per-frame hot paths.

variants.name: Framework signals hub (Django/blinker)
variants.implementation_notes: A framework signal dispatcher is the mediator as a library: define a Signal, receivers connect with connect() or the @receiver decorator, and the producer calls send(sender, **kwargs); the dispatcher owns the receiver registry, dispatch order and weak-reference handling. Django's implementation is the most widespread instance, and blinker is the standalone equivalent that backs Flask's signals. Use it when decoupled modules must react to another module's events without importing it; prefer a direct call or a plain mediator when the coordination has real request/response logic, because the Django documentation itself warns that signals look loosely coupled but quickly become hard to follow and debug.
variants.code_sketch:
from django.dispatch import Signal, receiver

order_submitted = Signal()          # the hub

@receiver(order_submitted)
def reserve_stock(sender, order, **kwargs):
    stock.reserve(order.items)

# producer — no knowledge of the receivers:
order_submitted.send(sender=checkout, order=order)
pitfalls: Receivers are stored as weak references by default, so a local function or unreferenced object is garbage-collected and the receiver silently stops firing; pass weak=False or keep a strong reference, and use dispatch_uid against duplicate registration.
send() runs receivers synchronously in registration order and returns their responses; a raising receiver propagates and stops the remaining ones.
Signals are broadcast with no return-value contract and no ordering guarantee between applications, so code that needs a decision back should call a mediator or a service directly.
Registration in AppConfig.ready() can run more than once during testing, so guard against duplicate receivers.
